societies.name: Fallout 76 — Watoga before the sabotage
societies.society: The functioning automated city’s resident and displaced human population

scope.period: The established pre-War city before Operation Free Watoga
scope.population: Living residents and people displaced or excluded by Watoga’s automation
exclusions: Post-War empty robot patrols as leisure citizens
All Appalachia as receiving city benefits

societies.description:
Watoga implements a largely automated municipal service system, while machine replacement drives unemployment and people out of the city. Access follows property wealth and corporate approval rather than a universal claim on the robot output. It is retained as an unequal automation-transition case: productive displacement is real, but displaced people do not thereby receive secure necessities. The high guarantee-axis value reflects costly residency, rejected applications and deliberately restricted services, rather than claiming every rich resident is deprived.

Corporate authorities and privileged residents shape admission and service policy. That supports concentrated human control despite extensive robot operation; an automated city is not automatically an AI sovereign. The scope precedes the sabotage and nuclear catastrophe, whose hostile patrols are a different condition. No nonworking fraction is inferred from unemployment: people may seek other jobs, care for others or undertake useful activity. The description also does not convert robot municipal services into proof that every commodity is produced locally or free of charge.

guarantees.basis: Automation displaces people while wealth and corporate approval restrict residence and services.

control.basis: Corporate admission decisions and elite service votes determine access; robot operation does not erase human policy control.

nonworking.basis: Unemployment and outmigration are not an all-person census of useful work.

evidence.claim: Actual automated services and unemployment coexist with corporate residency exclusion.
evidence.locator: Pre-War background and Operation Free Watoga

uncertainties: An unequal partial transition, not general freedom from subsistence work.
Municipal automation does not establish local automatic production of every good.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Fallout 3 — Vault 112’s active simulation captives
societies.society: Living long-term residents maintained in Tranquility loungers

scope.period: The continuing Braun-controlled simulation before player intervention
scope.population: Living longtime human residents with active simulated experiences
exclusions: Empty pods and simulated bystanders as additional humans
James and the player as representative permanent residents
Unconscious cryostasis residents of other vaults

societies.description:
Vault 112 keeps living residents inside continuing virtual experiences while machinery and caretaker Robobrains sustain the physical facility. They do not obtain bodily support through current outside employment. This is an actual long-running captive support unit, not merely stored data or an empty simulation. Its guarantee estimate is deliberately broad: bodily maintenance persists for generations, but residents cannot leave or hold their provider accountable. Virtual killings and memory resets are not automatically physical deaths, although the intervention that ends the experiment can make the threat real.

Control belongs to the human overseer Stanislaus Braun, rather than the maintenance robots or the residents collectively. Material support and severe coercion are recorded separately, with the possibility of withdrawal qualifying security. Active mental life does not imply that every resident performs no useful activity; simulated care and other meaningful work still count. No reliable participation census was found, so that axis remains unresolved. This record covers the established captive community before intervention, excluding temporary visitors, purely simulated neighbors and the dead population after a lethal failsafe.

guarantees.basis: Long-lasting physical support is real, but captives have no enforceable claim and lethal termination remains possible.

control.basis: Braun is a living human overseer controlling the simulation; caretaker robots do not establish an AI ruler.

nonworking.basis: Pod maintenance replaces external subsistence work, but active mental activity and useful simulated work are not censused.

evidence.claim: Robots maintain the vault while living humans remain in Braun-controlled active simulations.
evidence.locator: Vault background, caretaker maintenance and Tranquility Lounger description

uncertainties: Coercion is distinct from automatic withdrawal of bodily provision.
Physical residents, active experiences and simulated bystanders are distinguished.
No participation census or fixed resident count is invented.
The lethal ending is outside the provision period.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Deus Ex: Invisible War — ApostleCorp’s Helios Union
societies.society: Humanity in the realized ApostleCorp ending at Union year 125

scope.period: The narrated mature Union, 125 years after the ApostleCorp branch
scope.population: Living humanity linked through the universal nanite/Helios system
exclusions: The original Deus Ex merger as already achieving this order

societies.description:
The ApostleCorp ending goes beyond an immediate promise: its later narration reports completed economic automation and an enduring Union in which people’s needs are treated collectively. That supports a post-work material system, with a moderately strong guarantee estimate. The score remains uncertain because the short ending gives no detailed inventory of housing, care or possible exclusion. This is one realized player-selected branch, not the outcome of every playthrough or a claim that the original game’s merger already achieved the same economy.

Helios coordinates linked human minds and voices their consensus. The actual balance between shared human agency and the AI’s decisive authority is ambiguous, so control remains unresolved, with both AI provision and distributed-human provision interpretations recorded. Calling the link a democracy does not settle that balance. The ending explicitly preserves research, and freedom from necessary production work does not mean an absence of useful chosen activity. No nonworking percentage is supplied. Unused sequel plans and the other endings do not extend this branch’s constitution.

guarantees.basis: Completed economic automation and collective needs support a material floor, but the ending lacks detailed entitlements.

control.basis: Human consensus, a merged human leader and Helios coordination coexist; decisive productive agency is not resolved.

nonworking.basis: Economic automation coexists with continuing research; no all-person participation rate is given.

evidence.claim: The mature selected ending explicitly reports completed economic automation and collective needs.
evidence.locator: ApostleCorp ending narration at Union year 125; route and project context

uncertainties: Mutually exclusive realized branch, not universal canon.
AI versus linked-human effective control remains unresolved.
Research remains useful work; automation is not a participation census.
The material-floor estimate is an interpretation of brief ending narration.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

review_notes: Twelve ordered decisions and three records; short game summaries, ending narration and bounded passages only.
Watoga’s pre-sabotage displacement/exclusion is separated from post-War empty patrols. Unemployment is not converted into nonworking.
Vault 112 contains active living humans, unlike cryostasis. Braun remains a human ruler; virtual and physical death are distinguished.
ApostleCorp’s mature ending is explicit enough for admission. The ending’s shared agency remains ambiguous, not guessed from its democracy label.
Blocked Fallout terminal pages were respected. Unrelated Vault 111 excerpts and role-playing/fanfiction hits were discarded.
